title: ASASSN-14ko flares decayed 1.6 times more slowly and had 1.3-1.8 times more fluence in the 2020-2023 period stall than in decay orbits; a linear fluence period law fails out of sample
abstract: Question: the period decrease of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko stopped in 2020 and started again near 2023-2024. Clocks that act through the stripped mass or the gas near the black hole predict that the flares or the X-ray state change in the same orbits; random period kicks predict no change. Approach: we fitted an on-off clock to 22 single-marker times (X-ray deep suppression, optical half-rise) on a wide grid of break cycles, measured the soft X-ray state of each cycle from 688 Swift XRT and NICER visits, tested nine flare and X-ray series for changes at the breaks with change-point models and 1000 parametric bootstraps, fitted period laws driven by the per-orbit flare fluence with an out-of-sample check, and bounded the drag of the star's own debris. All inputs come from signed campaign publications. Results: the decrease stopped at cycle 21 (2020 December; 95%: 21-22) and restarted near cycle 30 (68%: 28-32). In the stall orbits the ASAS-SN g flares had 1.76 times more fluence (95%: 1.09-2.85; p = 0.010) and decayed more slowly than in the decay orbits before and after. Without the unusual 2022 flares, the three flares of cycles 21-24 still decayed 1.60 times more slowly (17.2 against 10.7 d) and had 1.30 times more fluence than the ten decay-orbit flares (Mann-Whitney p = 0.028 each). The decline time changed at the stop (x1.70, 1.28-2.27; p = 0.001). The soft X-ray low state (post-dip rate down about 3 times, recovery time from 6-11 d to 87-89 d, harder spectrum) started at cycles 27-28, six or seven orbits after the stop. A law in which more fluence lengthens the period fits the timing markers best (AIC 42.1 against 45.8 for the on-off clock) but predicts a period increase in 2022 that the unfitted UVW2 peaks of cycles 27-29 do not show (chi2 = 7.1-11.4 for 3 points). A threshold law (decay only in orbits with weak flares) fits as well as the on-off clock. Drag in the star's own debris gives at most 10 percent of the pre-stall decay. Conclusion: the stall coincides with stronger, longer flares, which argues against pure timing noise and against energy-proportional decay; the trigger is not identified. Limitations: 16 good g flares (3 in cycles 21-24), one parametric fit per flare, no correction for multiple tests, X-ray data only from 2020, interpolated fluences, three out-of-sample points, no data on the 2026 flares.
